1.pericope_label: Thirty-eight years round Mount Seir, and the turn north

schools.summary: Gill notes that in turning from Kadesh they set their backs to Canaan; Calvin values the verse for the join it makes with Numbers, which does not say when they struck camp, and reads the circuitous wandering as teaching them to follow God directly rather than decline from the way he points out.

Henry makes the delay purposeful on both sides — chastisement and preparation for Israel, whose souls were being made meet for heaven by a long train of exercises, and preparation of the Canaanites for destruction, since the years that might have been improved for repentance hardened them and made them secure.

Clarke contrasts this route with the earlier one by Kadesh-barnea, running between Edom on one side and Moab and Ammon on the other; Wesley glosses Mount Seir and puts the period at thirty-eight years.

Ellicott observes that the opening word is simply 'and', with no note of time, and speculates at length about when the decision to enter by way of Jordan rather than the south country was taken; Keil and Delitzsch trace the march through the Arabah and round the southern end of Seir.

4.pericope_label: Pass by Edom, and pay for what you take

schools.summary: Gill and Aben Ezra read the permission to buy as conditional on their choosing to, since the manna still fell; Calvin measures how hard the charge was — not only was the embassy foreknown to be fruitless, but even hostility was to be met without arms, which left Israel worse off than the common law of nations allowed, and he takes their bearing it as evidence of how far chastisement had subdued them.

Clarke has God give them property so that they needed no spoil and could pay; Wesley forbids the appetite rather than the purchase, explains the buying of water by its scarcity, and calls theft inexcusable in men who could not plead necessity.

Ellicott reads the clause literally as 'ye are passing through the border', refers the Edomites' fear to the song of Moses, notes that Esau's inheritance was won before Jacob's as Ishmael's line developed before Isaac's, and sees nothing unreasonable in supposing Israel acquired wealth by trade or ordinary occupations on the road.

debates.question: How could God be said to have blessed the work of their hands in the desert?

sides.position: their cattle increased and their daily labour yielded furniture and necessaries, though they earned no wages
they may simply have acquired wealth by trade and ordinary occupations, having skilled workmen among them

themes: how a wandering people grew rich

8.pericope_label: Past Moab, and who held these lands before

schools.summary: Gill traces the Emim to the campaign of Chedorlaomer and derives their name from the terror they inspired, and cannot say who the Horim were beyond supposing them cave-dwellers of southern Idumea, the Troglodytes of the Greeks; Calvin marks the parenthesis, notes that God's favour rested not on what these nations deserved but on their descent from Lot, and observes how much harder the second prohibition was to keep than the first.

Henry stops on the word 'brethren' used of a people who had just refused Israel passage, and makes the rule general: when our relations fail in their duty to us we must keep a sense of the relation and not fail in ours.

Clarke resists the whole picture of giants — the word is not giants but Rephaim, the name of a people, and Emim, Anakim and Rephaim were probably one race under different names, a hardy plundering people to whom fear and public report added stature; Wesley reads the expulsion of the Emim as encouragement, since God would much more drive out the Canaanites.

Keil and Delitzsch trace the route by Elath and Ezion-geber and find in the terms 'brethren' and 'sons of Lot' a bond of blood-relationship to be held sacred; Ellicott notes that the children of Lot, like those of Ishmael and Esau, had their inheritance before Abraham's did.

debates.question: Were the Emim and Rephaim giants?

sides.position: a race of great stature, terrible enough to name a people after the fear they caused
Rephaim is the name of a people, not a word for giants; they were plunderers to whom report added height

themes: who dug the caves of Seir

13.pericope_label: The brook Zered, and a generation wasted out

schools.summary: Gill notes that the word carries both valley and brook and places it near Dibon-gad, and itemises the judgments that consumed the generation — the sword of Amalek, the plague at Shittim, Korah's destruction and the plague that followed; Calvin reads the halt as forbidding advance until God opened the way, and explains that men of war means those above twenty, the forty years elsewhere including the two spent at Sinai.

Ellicott admits the brook is unidentified but derives its name from the pruning of willows and turns it into a figure of the vine purged that it might bring more fruit; he reads the notice as evidence of intimate knowledge of the exodus and imagines the survivors as marked men who knew they had a short time to live. Keil and Delitzsch date the crossing from the condemnation at Kadesh and connect the hand of the Lord with the terrors by which he destroys his enemies.

themes: not all by a natural death
the last of the marked men

schools.summary: Gill locates the crossing at Ar on the Arnon; Calvin faces the difficulty that two nations born of an incestuous connection should be favoured above the common lot, refuses to explain it and calls God's judgments a deep abyss to be regarded with reverence, then argues that Ammon's overthrow of giants proves the same special favour, and admits he cannot settle where those giants came from.
Ellicott records Conder's identification of Ar; Keil and Delitzsch tie the fresh command to the dying out of the condemned generation and mark the Ammonite limit as ground already granted.

outliers.claim: the disgraceful act committed in drunkenness was marked with perpetual infamy and still left signs of mercy on it, chiefly for Abraham’s sake

themes: a guess offered as a guess

schools.summary: Gill has the Zamzummim too numerous and too tall for Ammon to have prevailed unaided, identifies the Avim with the Avites who held Philistine country as far as Gaza, and reads their place-name as courts, meaning huts set round an open square.

Clarke calls the territory the land of the Rephaim, identifies the Zamzummim with the Zuzim, and reduces these peoples to inconsiderable clans pursuing and pursued until a stronger power absorbed them; he also observes that these two blocks of verses stand apart from the narrative as a single interpolated survey. Wesley makes the Caphtorim kin to the Philistines, confederate with them and merged with them by marriage, and takes Caphtor for Cappadocia.

Ellicott would render the place-name 'in villages' rather than treat it as proper, glosses Azzah as Gaza, reports Cyprus or Crete as candidates for Caphtor, notes that the verse makes Philistia itself the scene of a conquest, and draws the argument the passage exists for — that if Lot's, Ishmael's and Esau's children could dispossess such races, how much more Israel under God's own guidance.

themes: clans that pursued and were pursued

24.pericope_label: Cross Arnon and contend with Sihon

schools.summary: Gill hears in the promised dread the fulfilment of what Moses prophesied at the sea; Calvin holds that the order of events has been inverted, taking the embassy of the following verses as a parenthesis to be read in the pluperfect, so that the commission to attack came only after the messengers had returned empty and the war was therefore lawful.

Henry reads the commission as a recompense for the self-denial just shown, insists that what God gives we must still endeavour to get, and enters in advance the distinction that keeps the coming slaughter from being a precedent — Israel acted as executioners of God's wrath on a nation whose iniquity was full, and those will have judgment without mercy who show no mercy.
Wesley restricts the nations under the whole heaven to those who heard the report.

Ellicott notes that the land in question had been taken from Moab by the Amorites in the first place and sets the promised dread beside the song of Moses; Keil and Delitzsch contrast the kindred tribes with the Amorites who had forced their way into Gilead and Bashan, and hold that the offer of peace was seriously meant even though its refusal was foreseen.

debates.question: Did the embassy to Sihon precede or follow the command to attack?

sides.position: it preceded; the verses about it are a parenthesis to be read in the pluperfect
the order stands as written; the peace offer was made after the grant, to leave Sihon inexcusable

themes: why a precedent it is not

26.pericope_label: Words of peace, and a hardened spirit

schools.summary: Gill places Kedemoth by a wilderness of the same name, reports Aben Ezra's alternative, and follows Jarchi in noting that what Edom and Moab had actually granted was the sale of food and drink rather than a passage.

Wesley catches the force of 'on my feet', a company going on foot rather than an army of horsemen, which would have been far more dangerous to admit; he finds the favour ascribed to the people of Esau rather than to their king, and glosses the hardening as God suffering the spirit to be hardened.

Ellicott reads the message against the later law of sieges, by which the offer of terms excepted Sihon from the doomed nations so that he brought his fate on himself, and refuses to soften the hardening — God gave Sihon his strength as he gave Pharaoh his, and the same verb that makes a heart obstinate here tells Joshua to be of good courage; Keil and Delitzsch call it a judgment of hardening suspended over him.

debates.question: What does it mean that God hardened Sihon’s spirit?

sides.position: God suffered it to be hardened
a judgment of hardening laid on him, leading to his destruction
God gave him the strength; hardening is no more a moral process than the hardening of steel, and the same gift made Joshua courageous

33.pericope_label: The city laid under the ban

schools.summary: Gill has the Lord deliver Sihon with his lands, names the cities taken, and marks the one exception to the destruction, the cattle kept alive as the conquerors' own property.
Wesley grounds the extermination in the express command of the Lord of life and death against a people devoted for their abominable wickedness.

Ellicott notes that the Hebrew as written reads 'his son' rather than 'his sons', and insists the word for utter destruction will bear nothing less than devotion to destruction, so that the narrative asserts an extermination by God's express command; Keil and Delitzsch describe the ban laid on every town and read 'city of men' as the male town population, which makes the clauses about women and children an addition rather than a repetition.

themes: what the cattle were spared for

schools.summary: Gill makes Aroer the principal city on the Moabite border and lists what was left untouched — Ammon's actual holdings, the towns on the Jabbok, the cities of their mountain country, and whatever else God had forbidden.

Clarke reads the limits as proof that the commission was limited, only those being cut off whose iniquity was full, and follows the sequel into later history: Moab and Ammon requited the forbearance by fighting Israel and committing shocking cruelties, which is why they were afterwards barred from the congregation to the tenth generation. Wesley takes the phrase about the Jabbok to mean beyond it, that river being the Ammonite border.

Keil and Delitzsch read the two towns as the inclusive and exclusive termini of the land taken, with Gilead as the northern limit, and gloss 'too high' as too strong to be taken; Ellicott gives Conder's site for Aroer and openly questions why the same surveyor makes the Aroer of Numbers a different and unknown place.
